content: Mayonnaise, commonly referred to as mayo, is a thick condiment primarily made from vegetable oil and egg yolks. It has a whitish-yellow color and is a stable emulsion created by combining oil and egg yolks. The flavor is typically enhanced with lemon juice or vinegar, salt, and sometimes mustard. Various other sauces can be derived from mayonnaise by incorporating additional seasonings. The origin of the term mayonnaise is debated. One theory suggests it was brought to France from Mahon, Spain, after the French victory over the British at the port of Mahon in 1756. Marie-Antoine Carême later refined the recipe by emulsifying vegetable oil and egg yolks, making it lighter and popular across Europe. If this history is accurate, the Balearic version of aioli, known as allioli, may have inspired mayonnaise. The name mayonnaise might derive from Mahon (yielding mahonnaise) or the French word manier (meaning to stir or to blend, leading to magnonnaise). Another explanation from the 1961 Larousse Gastronomique suggests the name is a corruption of the old French word moyeunaise, derived from moyeu, meaning egg yolk. This aligns with the sauce's composition as an emulsion of egg yolks and oil. Other theories propose the name may have originated from Charles de Lorraine, Duke of Mayenne, who reportedly finished a meal with cold sauce before his defeat at the Battle of Arques. The Oxford English Dictionary notes that mayonnaise first appeared in English in an 1841 cookbook. Ambrose Bierce humorously described mayonnaise in his Devil's Dictionary as one of the sauces which serve the French in place of a state religion. Mayonnaise can be prepared using an electric mixer, blender, food processor, or manually with a whisk or fork. The process involves gradually adding oil to an egg yolk while whisking vigorously to disperse the oil. The oil and water in the yolks form the emulsion base, while lecithin in the yolks acts as the emulsifier, stabilizing the mixture. Mustard may also be added to enhance stability, as its small particles serve as nucleation sites for the droplets forming the emulsion. The traditional French recipe for mayonnaise uses high-quality olive oil and sometimes vinegar or lemon juice. Some modern recipes specify safflower oil. It is crucial to beat the mixture continuously while adding the olive oil drop by drop, ensuring each addition is fully incorporated before adding more. Experienced cooks can determine when the mayonnaise is ready by the resistance of the emulsion to the whisking action. Homemade mayonnaise may taste stronger or sharper than commercial varieties, and overworking olive oil can make it bitter. To avoid this, safflower oil is often used to create the initial emulsion, with olive oil added later using a wooden spoon instead of a whisk. Vegan mayonnaise options, such as soy-based products like Nayonaise and Vegenaise, are widely available and can also be made at home. Homemade mayonnaise can contain up to 85% fat before the emulsion breaks down, while commercial varieties typically range from 70-80% fat. Low-fat mayonnaise products use starches, cellulose gel, or other ingredients to mimic the texture of traditional mayonnaise. Some homemade recipes use whole eggs, including the whites, or even just egg whites, which can be emulsified at high speed in a food processor. The resulting texture and taste are similar to traditional mayonnaise when seasoned appropriately. Commercial producers often pasteurize or freeze the yolks, substitute water for most of the liquid, or use alternative emulsifiers. For homemade mayonnaise, the freshest eggs are recommended, and pasteurized eggs are available in some stores. Eggs can also be coddled in 170°F (77°C) water, with the slightly cooked yolks separated from the whites. Homemade mayonnaise typically lasts three to four days under refrigeration. Contrary to popular belief, mayonnaise's acidic pH prevents harmful bacterial growth, though it can develop an unpleasant taste and smell if left unrefrigerated. Globally, mayonnaise is commonly used in sandwiches, salads like potato salad, and dishes such as tuna salad. In the United States, commercial mayonnaise originated in New York City, with the first ready-made mayonnaise sold at Richard Hellmann's delicatessen in 1905. By 1912, Hellmann's Blue Ribbon Mayonnaise was mass-marketed. On the West Coast, Best Foods introduced its mayonnaise, which became popular. In 1932, Best Foods acquired the Hellmann's brand, preserving both due to their strong regional market shares. In the Southeastern U.S., Duke's Mayonnaise, created in 1917 by Eugenia Duke, remains a popular brand. Blue Plate Mayonnaise, produced by Reily Foods Company, is also widely consumed in the Southern U.S. In Europe, mayonnaise is often served with French fries, particularly in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Germany, and increasingly in the UK, France, and Spain. It is also paired with cold chicken or hard-boiled eggs in countries like the Netherlands, France, Poland, Ukraine, and the UK. European guidelines recommend mayonnaise contain at least 70% oil and 5% liquid egg yolk, though this is not legislated, and most brands exceed these levels. Japanese mayonnaise, typically made with apple cider vinegar or rice vinegar and a small amount of MSG, has a distinct flavor profile compared to Western mayonnaise. It is sold in soft plastic squeeze bottles and has a thinner texture. Variants with Japanese mustard (karashi) are also common. It is popular in dishes like okonomiyaki, takoyaki, and yakisoba, as well as with cooked vegetables or as a dip mixed with soy sauce or wasabi. In the Tōkai region, it is frequently used as a condiment for cold noodle salads. Kewpie is the most popular brand of Japanese mayonnaise, recognized by its Kewpie doll logo. In Russia, mayonnaise is highly popular and made with sunflower seed oil, giving it a distinctive flavor. A 2004 study revealed that Russia is the only European market where mayonnaise outsells ketchup by volume. Leading brands include Calvé (marketed by Unilever) and Sloboda (marketed by Efko). Russian-speaking countries also offer various commercial mayonnaise flavors, such as olive, quail-egg, and lemon. Chile is the world's third-largest per capita consumer of mayonnaise and the leading consumer in Latin America. Since the 1980s, Chileans have used mayonnaise on dishes like locos, hot dogs, French fries, and boiled potatoes. Mayonnaise serves as a base for many other sauces and salad dressings. For example, aioli is an olive-oil mayonnaise with garlic, while rouille is aioli with added red pepper or paprika. Tartar sauce combines mayonnaise with pickled cucumbers, onions, and sometimes capers, olives, or crushed hard-boiled eggs. Russian dressing, also known as Marie Rose sauce in Europe, mixes mayonnaise with tomato sauce or ketchup and yogurt or heavy cream. Thousand Island dressing blends mayonnaise with tomato sauce, sweet pickle relish, herbs, and spices, sometimes including chopped hard-boiled eggs. Variants like lime-flavored mayonnaise (mayonesa) are common in Mexican or Spanish groceries. Sauce rémoulade in classic French cuisine adds mustard, gherkins, capers, parsley, chervil, tarragon, and possibly anchovy essence to mayonnaise. Ranch dressing combines mayonnaise with buttermilk or sour cream, minced green onion, and other seasonings.
